archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A rhythm thrower who almost never runs and lives on intermediate and deep throws over the middle, carrying an offense whose ground game has stalled.

report.headline: Volume is the ground game's fault; the efficiency surge since Week 5 is his.
report.take:
Jordan Love is on pace for 4,945 passing yards, and his 290.9 a game ranks second among 49 qualifiers. That is up 65.5 yards a game on last season, but the rate stats explain it better than the raw total does. His yards per attempt is essentially unchanged from 2025, and his completion rate and CPOE are both down about three points. The extra yardage is mostly extra throws. Green Bay's rushing EPA ranks 31st of 32, the team passes more than situation predicts (7th), and Love himself barely runs: 23 rushing yards all year, down from 199 last season. He is less a different quarterback than a quarterback asked to do more.

The season splits into two halves. Over the first four weeks his CPOE was negative in three games, and he posted negative passing EPA against Minnesota and the Jets. The Vikings game was a 21-of-42 day with a 37.5% bad-throw rate under constant pressure. From Week 5 on he has been one of the best passers in the league: 0.328 EPA per dropback over the last five, 0.347 with a 12.3 CPOE over the last three, capped by a 23-of-29, 372-yard, +22.6 EPA game at New England. The profile behind it is consistent. Throws of 10+ air yards produce 0.646 EPA per attempt, the middle of the field returns 0.55, and Christian Watson is turning 74 targets into 0.611 EPA each.

The season line hides some soft spots. Short passing is ordinary: throws under 10 air yards add almost nothing, and screens and throws behind the line have cost him outright. His 15.2% bad-throw rate ranks 30th of 42, a step back from last year's 12.5%, though the early weeks inflate it. Close fourth quarters have gone badly, with negative EPA and two interceptions, although that is only 36 plays. The red zone is a mixed picture: 13 touchdowns, but slightly negative EPA. On the plus side, he is getting the ball out faster than ever (2.6 seconds, down 0.29 from last year). That is a big reason his sack rate sits at 4.7% against a league average of 7.3%.

Where it heads: his 2025 work, 5th in EPA per play and 8th in CPOE, says the recent accuracy is closer to who he is than the September version was, though a 12-point CPOE won't hold. The danger is the immediate environment. Two starting linemen are out, the backfield is gutted, and the next opponent owns the league's best pass defense and pass rush.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep middle throws
strengths.body: Throws of 10+ air yards are his whole engine. Intermediate passes carry a 61% success rate, and the middle of the field yields far more than either sideline. That fits a LaFleur offense built on crossers and seams, and it matches the passer he has been for three years. The deep numbers swing on a few completions, but the intermediate efficiency is a skill.

strengths.title: Faster clock, fewer sacks
strengths.body: His time to throw dropped to 2.6 seconds from last year's 2.89, and his sack rate ranks 11th of 49 while staying well below league average. Pressure turns into a sack only 19.7% of the time. He has gotten quicker without getting conservative, since his aggressiveness is flat year to year. This looks like a deliberate change that should hold.

strengths.title: Under-center play-action efficiency
strengths.body: On 66 under-center dropbacks he has posted 0.443 EPA with a 14.4 CPOE and no interceptions. In shotgun he is merely solid. The sample is modest, but the cause is believable: under-center looks sell the run, which opens the middle-field windows he already wins in. It does depend on the run game staying credible enough to bite on.

concerns.title: Accuracy wobbles under pressure
concerns.body: His 15.2% bad-throw rate ranks 30th of 42, after he was 14th last year. The worst of it came in Week 1 against Minnesota, when he was pressured on nearly half his dropbacks. Since October he has been sharp, so this reads more as a pressure-driven flaw than a lost skill. That matters because the pressure is about to come back.

concerns.title: Thin support around him
concerns.body: The run game ranks 31st in EPA. Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks are all on the report, and right tackle Travis Glover (100% of snaps) and guard Sean Rhyan (87%) are out. Screens and throws behind the line have already been a drain. This isn't his flaw, but it narrows what the offense can do around him and raises the share of plays he has to win.

concerns.title: Tight-game finishes
concerns.body: In close fourth quarters he has negative EPA, two interceptions and no touchdowns, and the no-huddle split is also flat. At 36 plays this is a hint rather than a verdict. Still, it showed up in the three-point loss at Detroit, and it is worth tracking against good defenses.

trend.note: His passing EPA went from negative in Weeks 1-2 to modestly positive in Weeks 3-4, then took off from Week 5. The last three games show his best accuracy of the year, a 12.3 CPOE, and that came against mid-to-low-ranked defenses.

nextGame.headline: The league's top pass defense, with two linemen missing
nextGame.body:
Minnesota ranks first in defensive EPA, pass EPA, success rate, hit rate and sack rate. It allows quarterbacks the fewest fantasy points in the league. These are the same Vikings who pressured Love on 47.8% of his dropbacks in Week 1 and forced a 37.5% bad-throw day, even as he piled up 387 empty yards. There are seams, though. WR1s have produced 0.44 EPA per target against them (27th), and their deep defense is only 11th. Offenses run against them at the league's highest rate over the norm. That isn't a weakness Green Bay can easily exploit with a 31st-ranked rush offense, but Minnesota's 29th-ranked explosive-run rate offers some hope.

Availability cuts against Love on his own line. Glover and Rhyan are both out, which is the worst possible week to lose a tackle and a guard. Jacobs and Lloyd are out too, leaving Brooks' possible return from IR as the main hope for a functional run game. The other side of the ledger helps the script. Minnesota will be without Kyler Murray and Jauan Jennings, and its offense already ranks 31st in EPA. That explains why Green Bay is a 4.5-point favorite despite a 41.5 total. A lead could let the Packers shorten the game, which caps his volume but also limits how often he faces obvious passing downs against that rush.

keyMatchups.title: Vikings rush vs. patched line
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota leads the league in both hit rate and sack rate. Green Bay is replacing two starting linemen, and this pass rush is what wrecked Love's accuracy in Week 1. His faster release is the counter, but expect his time to throw to shrink further and the short game to carry more of the load.

keyMatchups.title: Golden and Watson outside
keyMatchups.body: The one role that has hurt Minnesota is the WR1, while tight ends have been shut down (2nd stingiest). That points the passing game toward Matthew Golden and Watson rather than Tucker Kraft. Watson's efficiency per target makes him the likeliest source of a chunk play.

keyMatchups.title: Favored script, low total
keyMatchups.body: With Murray out and Minnesota's offense near the bottom of the league, Green Bay should play from ahead. Love's leading-by-9+ split is efficient, with a 5.3 CPOE. But a 41.5 total implies fewer possessions and a lower ceiling than his recent shootouts.

nextGame.watch: Whether the replacement right side holds up long enough for Love to hit intermediate middle throws, or whether the game shrinks to quick throws and sacks like Week 1.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume should stay. The run game is broken and the backfield is depleted into late November, so Green Bay will keep leaning on him, and the passing EPA ranks sixth as a team. The last three games of accuracy will cool. A double-digit CPOE doesn't last, but his 2025 profile supports something in the mid-single digits, not the early-season negatives. Expect roughly 255-300 passing yards and 1.6-2.3 touchdowns a game, with interceptions staying low given his career-best ball security trend. The return of Jacobs and the two linemen is the main lever for efficiency. A run game that works would make the under-center play-action looks pay off again.

What's likely to regress: the red-zone touchdown count is outpacing his red-zone efficiency, and the deep-ball EPA rests on 62 attempts with a 37% completion rate, so a few drops or misses swing it. What's sustainable: the quick release, the low sack rate, and the intermediate middle-field game he has won with for three seasons. He offers almost nothing as a runner, so his weekly floor depends entirely on the passing volume holding.
swingFactors: Return of Glover and Rhyan on the line
Jacobs' timeline and a functional run game
Whether the recent accuracy holds against top defenses

confidence.note: Nine starts with a clear role, but the split between a weak September and a hot October-November, plus line and backfield injuries, leaves real uncertainty.
